planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Newcastle needs under 300 chill hours, one of the lowest requirements of any commercially available apricot.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun, ideally on a slight slope or elevated site where cold air drains away from the blossoms during late-winter frosts. Newcastle needs under 300 chill hours, one of the lowest requirements of any apricot cultivar in commerce, allowing it to set a reliable crop in mild-winter zone 8-9 regions where most apricots fail from insufficient winter chilling. Fruit is medium and firm-fleshed, good for fresh eating as well as canning and drying, ripening mid-to-early season. As with other very-low-chill apricots, its early bloom remains vulnerable to a late cold snap even though the tree tolerates the region's warm winters well. The tree is generally self-fruitful.
sources: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Bulida is a rustic Spanish heirloom apricot with roughly 500 chill hours, adaptable and reliable where winter chilling is marginal.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun, ideally on a slight slope or elevated site where cold air drains away from the blossoms during late-winter frosts. Bulida, a long-cultivated Spanish heirloom apricot, bears large, golden-orange, sweet and juicy fruit on a rustic, adaptable tree with a history of reliable performance across variable climates. Its chill requirement, while not the lowest among apricots, is manageable in much of zone 8, and its tough, forgiving nature has kept it in cultivation for generations. As with other apricots, early bloom leaves the crop vulnerable to a late cold snap, so good air drainage at the planting site helps protect the flowers.
sources: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Tropic Gold needs around 350 chill hours and is self-fruitful, marketed specifically for mild-winter zone 7-9 gardens.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun, ideally on a slight slope or elevated site where cold air drains away from the blossoms during late-winter frosts. Tropic Gold was bred and marketed specifically for mild-winter regions, needing only about 350 chill hours to set a reliable crop, bearing medium-to-large, firm, juicy, orange-fleshed fruit on a self-fruitful tree that needs no separate pollinizer. As with other low-chill apricots, its early bloom leaves the crop vulnerable to a late cold snap even though the tree itself tolerates the region's warm winters well.
sources: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Floragold needs about 400 chill hours or less and was bred as a reliable low-chill backyard producer, ripening two to three weeks before Blenheim.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun, ideally on a slight slope or elevated site where cold air drains away from the blossoms during late-winter frosts. Floragold was bred specifically as a dependable low-chill backyard apricot, needing roughly 400 chill hours or less and ripening two to three weeks ahead of the classic Blenheim, with all-purpose freestone fruit good for fresh eating and preserving. As with other low-chill apricots, its early bloom leaves the crop vulnerable to a late cold snap even though the tree itself tolerates the region's warm winters well.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Earligold needs roughly 250-400 chill hours and is one of the earliest-ripening apricots suited to mild-winter climates.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun, ideally on a slight slope or elevated site where cold air drains away from the blossoms during late-winter frosts. Earligold, needing only roughly 250 to 400 chill hours, is among the earliest-ripening apricot cultivars available, well suited to climates with minimal winter cold accumulation, giving gardeners the first fresh apricots of the season in a favorable year. As with other low-chill apricots, its early bloom leaves the crop vulnerable to a late cold snap even though the tree itself tolerates the region's warm winters well.
sources: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources

common_name: Castlebrite Apricot (Self-Fruitful Blushed-Red Reliable Early Bearer)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Castlebrite needs about 500 chill hours, is self-fruitful, and bears bright orange fruit blushed with red.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun, ideally on a slight slope or elevated site where cold air drains away from the blossoms during late-winter frosts. Castlebrite is self-fruitful and bears bright orange fruit blushed with red, semi-sweet in flavor, on a tree noted for reliably early and consistent bearing once established. Its chill requirement of roughly 500 hours suits it to the milder parts of zone 8 as well as zone 7. As with other apricots, early bloom leaves the crop vulnerable to a late cold snap, so good air drainage at the planting site helps protect the flowers.
sources: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources

common_name: Danube Cherry (Hungarian Duke-Type Sweet-Tart Cherry for Zone 9)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Danube is a Hungarian duke-type cherry (a natural sweet-sour hybrid) needing roughly 450 chill hours, among the very few named cherries explicitly marketed as workable in zone 9.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, choosing a site with good air drainage to reduce spring frost risk to the early flowers. Danube, a Hungarian duke-type cherry combining sweet and sour cherry parentage, was introduced to American growers by cherry breeder Amy Iezzoni and needs only about 450 chill hours, unusually low for a cherry, making it one of the very few named cherry cultivars explicitly marketed as workable at the northern edge of zone 9. It is partially self-fertile and ripens in early July, with balanced sweet-tart flavor typical of duke cherries. As with other low-chill stone fruit at the edge of their range, true performance under Gulf Coast humidity and disease pressure is less proven than in drier low-desert climates, so treat as a promising trial selection.
sources: Michigan State University — Amy Iezzoni cherry breeding program
University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources

common_name: Orient Nanking Cherry (Historic Self-Fertile Large-Fruited Bush Cherry)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Orient is a 1925 University of Minnesota self-fertile Nanking cherry selection with large oval fruit, a heat-tolerant bush cherry substitute for true cherries in the Deep South.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Orient, a self-fertile Nanking cherry selection released by the University of Minnesota in 1925, bears unusually large, oval, sweet-tart red fruit on a vigorous, dense, multi-stemmed shrub, offering a genuinely heat-tolerant bush-cherry alternative to true sweet and sour cherries, which generally fail in the Deep South's mild winters and humid summers. Ripening in early summer, the fruit is excellent fresh, for jam, or for wine, though birds compete heavily for the crop. Prune lightly after fruiting to maintain an open, productive form, since Nanking cherry blooms and fruits on one-year-old wood.
sources: University of Minnesota historic fruit breeding records

common_name: Drilea Nanking Cherry (Historic Upright Annual-Bearing Bush Cherry)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Drilea is a historic named Nanking cherry selection, upright-spreading and a reliable annual bearer with firm sweet round red fruit.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Drilea, a historic named Nanking cherry selection documented in USDA and nursery literature, bears firm, sweet, round red fruit on an upright-spreading, reliably annual-bearing shrub, ripening in mid-July, later than many other Nanking cherry selections. It offers a genuinely heat-tolerant bush-cherry alternative to true sweet and sour cherries, which generally fail in the Deep South's mild winters and humid summers, though it is now rarely commercially available and best sourced from specialty or heritage fruit nurseries. Prune lightly after fruiting to maintain an open, productive form, since Nanking cherry blooms and fruits on one-year-old wood.
